passed.title: Series.append mutates the Series in place
passed.trap: Unlike pandas habits where appending returns a new object, `Series.append` modifies the calling Series in place. It returns that same object only for convenience. Code like `c = a.append(b)` therefore also changes `a`, and the result is left with several chunks. Use `pl.concat([a, b])` to get a new Series and leave the original unchanged.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
b = pl.Series("a", [4, 5])
result = a.append(b)
print(a.to_list())  # a itself was mutated: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(result is a)  # True
print(a.n_chunks())  # 2

a2 = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
combined = pl.concat([a2, b])
print(a2.to_list())  # unchanged: [1, 2, 3]
print(combined.to_list())  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

passed.title: all/any skip nulls by default, so an all-null column reports True for all
passed.trap: By default, `Series.all` and `Series.any` use `ignore_nulls=True` and drop nulls before deciding. A column of only nulls then gives `True` from `Series.all` and `False` from `Series.any`, which can hide missing data. Pass `ignore_nulls=False` to get Kleene logic: the answer becomes `None` when nulls make the result unknown. Both methods only work on Boolean data, so build a mask first, for example `s > 0`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series([None, True], dtype=pl.Boolean)
print(s.all())  # True: the null is ignored
print(s.all(ignore_nulls=False))  # None: unknown

nulls = pl.Series([None, None], dtype=pl.Boolean)
print(nulls.all(), nulls.any())  # True False
print(nulls.all(ignore_nulls=False), nulls.any(ignore_nulls=False))  # None None

f = pl.Series([None, False], dtype=pl.Boolean)
print(f.any(), f.any(ignore_nulls=False))  # False None
passed.output:
True
None
True False
None None
False None

passed.title: arg_sort puts nulls first by default
passed.trap: `Series.arg_sort` defaults to `nulls_last=False`, so the positions of nulls come first in the result. Code that takes `s.arg_sort()[0]` as the position of the smallest value gets the null instead. Pass `nulls_last=True` when you want nulls at the end. Use `Series.arg_min` if you only need the position of the minimum.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [3, None, 1, 2])
print(s.arg_sort().to_list())  # [1, 2, 3, 0] -> null position first
print(s.arg_sort()[0])  # 1: the null, not the minimum
idx = s.arg_sort(nulls_last=True)
print(idx.to_list())  # [2, 3, 0, 1]
print(s.gather(idx).to_list())  # [1, 2, 3, None]
print(s.arg_min())  # 2

passed.title: arg_max/arg_min return a position or None, not an index label
passed.trap: Polars has no index, so `Series.arg_max` and `Series.arg_min` return a 0-based integer position. This is not a pandas-style `idxmax` label. Nulls are skipped, and the return type is `int | None`. A Series with no non-null values gives `None`, so check for `None` before passing the result on to indexing or `Series.gather`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, None, 3, 2])
print(s.arg_max(), s.arg_min())  # 2 0 -> positions, nulls skipped

empty = pl.Series("a", [None, None], dtype=pl.Int64)
pos = empty.arg_max()
print(pos)  # None
if pos is not None:
    print(empty[pos])
else:
    print("no non-null values")

passed.title: bottom_k output is unordered and only includes nulls when it has to
passed.trap: `Series.bottom_k` and `Series.bottom_k_by` do not promise any order in their output. Call `sort` afterwards if order matters, and do not treat the first element as the minimum. Non-null elements are always chosen ahead of nulls, regardless of `reverse`. Nulls only appear when `k` is larger than the number of non-null values.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [2, None, 5, 1, None])
print(s.bottom_k(3).sort().to_list())  # [1, 2, 5]: nulls are not 'smallest'
print(s.bottom_k(4).sort(nulls_last=True).to_list())  # [1, 2, 5, None]

passed.title: Out-of-domain trig results are NaN or inf, not null
passed.trap: Out-of-domain inputs return NaN, not null. `Series.arccosh` gives NaN below 1, and `Series.arctanh` gives NaN when the absolute value is above 1, `inf` at 1 and `-inf` at -1. `Series.null_count` reports 0 for these NaNs and `Series.drop_nulls` keeps them, so check with `is_nan()` or `is_finite()` instead. Use `fill_nan(None)` to turn NaN into nulls, or `drop_nans()` to remove them.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [5.0, 1.0, 0.0, -1.0]).arccosh()
print(s.null_count())  # 0
print(s.drop_nulls().len())  # 4: NaNs survive
print(s.is_nan().sum())  # 2
print(s.fill_nan(None).null_count())  # 2
print(s.drop_nans().to_list())

t = pl.Series("b", [1.0, 0.5]).arctanh()
print(t.to_list(), t.is_finite().to_list())  # [inf, ...] [False, True]

passed.title: ceil returns floats, not integers
passed.trap: `Series.ceil` rounds up but keeps the floating-point dtype. The result is `2.0`, not `2`, and it is documented to work only on floating-point Series. If later code needs integers, for example for `Series.gather` or for a join key, cast explicitly with `.cast(pl.Int64)`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1.2, 2.5, -1.5])
c = s.ceil()
print(c.dtype)  # Float64
print(c.to_list())  # [2.0, 3.0, -1.0]
ci = c.cast(pl.Int64)
print(ci.dtype, ci.to_list())  # Int64 [2, 3, -1]

passed.title: cast is strict by default; strict=False silently turns failures into nulls
passed.trap: `Series.cast` defaults to `strict=True`, so a single unparsable string or out-of-range number makes the whole cast raise. Setting `strict=False` does not fix the data: it turns every invalid value into null without any warning, so check `Series.null_count` afterwards. For numeric overflow, `wrap_numerical=True` wraps the value around instead of failing or producing null. Choose that option deliberately, because it returns a different number rather than flagging the problem.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series(["1", "2", "x"])
try:
    s.cast(pl.Int64)
except Exception:
    print("strict string cast raised")
lenient = s.cast(pl.Int64, strict=False)
print(lenient.to_list(), lenient.null_count())  # [1, 2, None] 1

big = pl.Series([1, 300])
try:
    big.cast(pl.UInt8)
except Exception:
    print("strict overflow cast raised")
print(big.cast(pl.UInt8, strict=False).to_list())  # [1, None]
print(big.cast(pl.UInt8, wrap_numerical=True).to_list())  # [1, 44]
passed.output:
strict string cast raised
[1, 2, None] 1
strict overflow cast raised
[1, None]
[1, 44]
